Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

solomonR (development version)

HC3 standard errors at leverage 1 (bug fix, #173)

  • Under the default robust = "HC3", fit_solomon_glm() failed when a participant’s leverage (hat value) was 1. This happens when the pretest varies within the pretested groups only through one participant, or when a covariate varies only through one participant, such as a factor level that one participant alone holds. HC3 divides each participant’s squared residual by (1 - h)^2, so that participant’s term is 0/0, and the HC3 standard error of every estimate that depends on the participant is undefined (MacKinnon & White, 1985). A Gaussian fit with a pretest stopped with R’s internal error “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”. Other families, and Gaussian fits without a pretest, returned NaN for every standard error, with only a warning from the sandwich package. With a numeric covariate, the standard errors depended on rounding, without a warning. fit_solomon_mi() gave Inf, NaN, or rounding-dependent standard errors without a warning, and so did the delta method of marginal_solomon().
  • These fits now report each estimate that depends on such a participant with NA for its standard error, statistic, p-value, interval, and Wald R-squared. They give one warning of class solomonR_hc3_leverage_warning, which names the participants by their row numbers in the data, states the likely cause, and suggests robust = "none". A participant is taken to be at leverage 1 when the hat value is above 1 - 10^-8. An estimate in which the participant’s weight is at most 10^-8 times the largest weight does not depend on the participant; it keeps its HC3 standard error, with the participant’s term at its limit, 0. In the issue’s example, the treatment effect among unpretested participants keeps its HC3 standard error, 2.273. The HC3 covariance then comes from the model’s QR decomposition. The fit returns the row numbers as hc3_leverage, and the entries of vcov and of covariate_scaling$vcov that depend on the participant are NA.
  • The same rule applies to designs with several treatments and their omnibus tests, to the pretest effects at both centers, to fit_solomon_mi(), to the delta method of marginal_solomon(), and to the cell means of plot_sensitization(). A delta-method result of marginal_solomon() carries the fit’s hc3_leverage. report_solomon() gives the affected estimates without an interval or test and, when it reports such an estimate, says why. plot_solomon_effects() leaves them out and names them in its caption, rather than as contrasts the model does not estimate. plot_sensitization() names the cell means without an interval in its caption, and its subtitle says when the Pretest x Treatment estimate, or with several treatments the Pretest x Condition test, has no interval or result. equivalence_solomon(), equivalence bounds in the plots, and tipping_point_solomon() stop with an error for such a contrast. perm_solomon() is not changed; issue #134 covers it.
  • With several treatments, a comparison without a p-value, as when its HC3 standard error is undefined, counts in the adjustment of the other comparisons of its contrast by Holm’s (1979) or the Bonferroni procedure, as if its p-value were the largest. The adjustment is then across the number of comparisons that the print and the report state. The same rule applies to the treatments’ pretest effects, at both centers.
  • report_solomon() gives an estimate that has no interval and no p-value as the estimate followed by “(no interval or test is available)”, rather than with an interval and a p-value of NA. This holds in the sentences that give the rows of a result’s effects table with their intervals, and for the pretest effects at the other center. It holds in analyses without a participant at leverage 1 too, such as a marginal_solomon() bootstrap that gives no interval, or a CR2 fit that gives no standard errors at the other center.
  • The refusal of HC3 for a group with a single analyzable participant now has the class solomonR_hc3_singleton_error, on the four-group and the several-treatment paths, with the same message, so that a script can catch it by its class. fit_solomon_mi() had no such refusal and gave standard errors that depended on rounding; it now stops with the same error.

Refits under the fit’s contrasts (bug fix, #168)

  • marginal_solomon() and plot_sensitization() refit the model of a fit_solomon_glm() fit, and the refit coded a factor covariate by the contrasts option (options("contrasts")) in force when they ran, not as the fit had coded it. They combined the refit with the fit’s coefficients and covariance, so when the two codings differed, their results were wrong, without an error or a warning. This happened to a fit with a factor, logical, or character covariate made under one option and analyzed under another: for instance, a fit made after options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly")), saved with saveRDS(), and analyzed in a new session, or the reverse. An ordered factor was affected when the second element of the option differed. A fit analyzed under the option it was made under was not affected, nor was a factor with contrasts of its own, set with contrasts(), unless one of its levels had no participants in the model: R then drops the factor’s own contrasts and codes it by the option.

  • In marginal_solomon(), for a binary, Poisson, or negative-binomial fit with a pretest or a numeric covariate:

    • The estimates standardized over the pretested participants in the model (pretest_center = "analyzed", the default) were wrong, both in the main results and in pretest_sensitivity. In the issue’s example, the average treatment effect was a risk difference of 0.0475 instead of 0.0414. The estimates standardized over every pretested participant with a pretest (pretest_center = "observed") were right. When no pretested participant was outside the model, the two standardizations are of the same participants, and pretest_sensitivity repeated the main results under both labels, so its rows were right or wrong with them.
    • The delta-method standard errors were wrong under either center (in the example, 0.0764 instead of 0.0648), with one exception: for a CR2 fit with a pretest but no numeric, date, or time covariate, under pretest_center = "observed", only those of the pretest effects were wrong (and the degrees of freedom of every contrast, as below).
    • With the default center, the bootstrap refitted each resample on the design of the refitted model, starting from the fit’s coefficients, which belong to the fit’s coding. Whether a refit converged then depended on that start, so some resamples failed that would have been used, or the reverse. Often more than 10% of them failed; the function then warned that the logistic fit had failed in that many resamples and reported no intervals, and the standard errors were wrong or missing. When fewer failed, it reported intervals without a warning, but its standard errors and limits were right only when the same resamples failed as under the fit’s coding, and even then they were the intervals of the right estimate, not of the reported one. The bootstrap standard errors and limits with pretest_center = "observed" were right.
    • With robust = "CR2", the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom were wrong too.
    • For a Poisson or negative-binomial fit, the rate ratios of Pretest x Treatment, Treatment | pretested, and Treatment | unpretested, and their standard errors, were right under either center: each depends on the treatment coefficients alone. The other contrasts were wrong as above.

  • In marginal_solomon(), for a CR2 fit with no pretest and no numeric covariate, the degrees of freedom of every contrast and the standard errors of the pretest effects were wrong; the estimates were right. Without CR2, such a fit was not affected.

  • In plot_sensitization(), for a CR2 fit with one treatment or several, the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom of the cell means, and so their intervals, were wrong. The means and their standard errors were right.

  • The refits now pass the fit’s contrasts (fit$model$contrasts) to glm() and, for a negative-binomial fit, to MASS::glm.nb(), so the contrasts option in force when they run no longer changes how they code a covariate. A fit analyzed under the option it was made under gives the same results as before. Tests fit under contr.sum and analyze under the default option, and the reverse, and check that the results equal those of a fit made and analyzed under the default.

  • perm_solomon() also refits the model under the option in force. Its statistic uses only the treatment coefficients and their variance, which do not depend on how a covariate is coded, so its results were right; it is unchanged. The refits inside fit_solomon_glm() run under the option of the fit.

Bootstrap refits on ill-conditioned designs (#154)

  • Refits that rounding error kept from converging are fitted again. marginal_solomon() refits each bootstrap resample by iteratively reweighted least squares, which stops when the deviance changes by less than 1e-8 of itself within 25 iterations, the rule of glm.fit(). With nearly collinear covariates, the condition number of the design can reach 1e14. Rounding error then moves the deviance by more than the rule allows at every iteration. On the nested covariates of #154, with a binary outcome and R = 199, 199, 197, and 195 resamples failed, the intervals were not reported, and the warning blamed sparse cells. A refit that does not converge is now fitted again with the intercept, the pretesting indicator, the pretest, and the covariates replaced by the orthonormal columns of their QR decomposition (Golub, 1965). These span the same space, and the treatment terms are kept, so in exact arithmetic it is the same fit (Green, 1984). On those data no resample fails, and the standard errors are within 0.1% of those of an exact reparameterization. That agreement is for those data. The new columns are computed in floating point, so a refit in them is accurate to about the unit roundoff times the condition number of the columns they replace, as the model’s own fit is (Higham, 2002), and under near separation a resample can be counted as failed, or not, differently than in an exact reparameterization. The convergence rule is unchanged.
  • A refit whose design is not of full rank is not fitted again. It still counts as failed, as when a resample lacks a level of a factor or makes nearly collinear covariates collinear. In the new columns, a direction that a resample makes collinear is carried only by rounding error, and a refit could converge on it.
  • A refit that did not converge is checked by the collinearity check of fit_solomon_glm() before it is fitted again. Rounding error can keep a design that is not of full rank above the tolerance of qr(), 1e-11, as when a covariate is computed from others. Take a time of testing that is the time of enrollment plus a delay, in seconds since 1970, except for two participants whose testing time was corrected. A resample without those two has the relation on every row, and its refit does not converge. Fitted again in the new columns, all 43 such resamples of 199 would converge, with risk differences up to 0.088 from those of the same refit without the delay, and the intervals would be reported where an exact reparameterization of the covariates withholds them. So the resample of a refit that did not converge is first checked by the collinearity check of fit_solomon_glm(), applied to its rows with the weights of the model’s fit. If a term is collinear with the others by that check, the resample counts as failed, as a design not of full rank, and is not fitted again. On those data, the bootstrap fails in the same resamples as the exact reparameterization and withholds the intervals. Before this change, those resamples failed too, as refits that did not converge, and the intervals were withheld. A refit that converged is not checked.
  • The cost is a band just inside the collinearity check of fit_solomon_glm(). There, rounding error can make nearly collinear covariates collinear on some resamples, to within the tolerance of qr() or by the check, and these resamples fail too. In one example, with z2 = z1 + 1.2e-11 * e1 and seed = 2024, 87 of 199 resamples failed before. The 63 that did not converge now converge in the new columns, and the 24 whose design fell short of full rank still fail, where an exact reparameterization of the covariates has no failures. At z2 = z1 + 1.1e-11 * e1, 3 of the 34 that did not converge are collinear by the check and fail. With other seeds, the check also stops a few such refits from z2 = z1 + 1.15e-11 * e1 up to at least z2 = z1 + 1.4e-11 * e1, about 30% above where fit_solomon_glm() stops, though rarely that far. A resample can also fail as a design not of full rank, as before, when only one of its participants departs from a relation that holds among the covariates of the others: the refit moves that participant’s fitted risk toward the outcome, and the participant’s weight vanishes. The new columns are formed whenever fit_solomon_glm() fitted the model, which it does only when no term is collinear with the others.
  • Results are unchanged where every refit converges. A refit that converges is computed as before, so on well-conditioned data the estimates, standard errors, intervals, p-values, and failure counts are identical. A test checks that such a bootstrap refits each resample once, on the model’s design.
  • The bootstrap warning gives the failures by reason. When more than 10% of the resamples fail, the warning counts those with a Solomon cell of only events or only non-events, a fitted risk within 1e-8 of 0 or 1, a design not of full rank, and no convergence in 25 iterations. It names the causes only of the reasons that occurred: sparse cells for the first; for the second, complete or quasicomplete separation (Albert & Anderson, 1984) or near separation, extreme covariate values, or a refit that diverged, since each refit takes full steps, without the step halving of glm.fit() (Marschner, 2011). A refit whose weighted design loses rank because fitted risks within 1e-8 of 0 or 1 make their weights vanish counts as a fitted risk near 0 or 1, not as a design short of full rank. For the refits that did not converge, the warning gives the largest condition number of their weighted design, with which rounding error grows (Higham, 2002). It no longer says that the failures are usually due to sparse cells. A covariate nearly collinear with a treatment term can still keep refits from converging, because the treatment terms, whose coefficients give the contrasts, are kept.
  • A fit that stops at the checks for an empty group, a collinear term, or a single participant under HC3 no longer gives the model fit’s warnings. fit_solomon_glm(), with one treatment or several, now holds back the warnings of its model fit until those checks have passed. Before, a negative-binomial fit with exactly collinear covariates warned that glm.fit() and theta did not converge, and then stopped with the error that a covariate is collinear. The warnings about the data given, raised before the fit, such as those about missing pretests, still come before the error. A fit that goes ahead gives the same warnings, in the same order, and the same results. A fit that stops inside glm() itself still gives its warnings before its error, as before. With several treatments, the noncollapsibility warning also waits for the checks.
  • model$converged describes the fit as given. ?fit_solomon_glm now says that, with a pretest or a numeric covariate, model$converged and model$iter describe the fit to the covariates and the pretest as given, not the standardized fit that gives the warnings.

Only MLR and ML in the SEM functions (#133)

  • A change in behavior. fit_solomon_sem(), fit_solomon_sem_latent(), and invariance_solomon() now accept only estimator = "MLR", the default, and "ML", in upper or lower case, and store the name in upper case, as invariance_solomon() prints it. Any other value, such as "MLM", "MLMV", "WLS", "GLS", "ULS", "DLS", or "RBM", now stops with an error that names the two and says that other estimators can be fitted with lavaan directly. Before, the functions passed any value to lavaan. MLR and ML are the estimators of the posted validation protocols. The protocol for fit_solomon_sem() on #117 restricts estimator to them. The amendment of October 9, 2026, on #55 studies the latent contrasts of fit_solomon_sem_latent() under both. In the invariance check it plans to validate, the test does not depend on estimator: the scaled difference (Satorra & Bentler, 2001) is always computed from MLR fits, and among the tests compared is the unscaled difference from the same fits, which equals the difference that invariance_solomon() gives under ML. invariance_solomon() accepts the estimators of fit_solomon_sem_latent(), which runs it. The functions fit with full-information maximum likelihood (missing = "fiml"), with which lavaan refuses MLM and MLMV, so neither could be fitted, although ?invariance_solomon named both.
  • The difference test is labeled by the fitted models. invariance_solomon() decided from the estimator’s name whether its chi-square difference test was scaled. With estimator = "mlr", lavaan computed the scaled test (Satorra & Bentler, 2001), and the printout and the report called it the unscaled one. The scaled test is now computed, and scaled is TRUE, when every model has a test with a scaling factor, the rule of #130; otherwise the unscaled test is computed. The printout and the report take the label from the fitted models too, not from the stored scaled, so a result saved before this change with "mlr", which stored scaled = FALSE, is now labeled scaled. The printout uses the stored scaled only when it cannot read the fitted models: when lavaan is not installed, or when the result no longer holds the three of them.
  • Reports. report_solomon() describes MLR and ML fits only. With three indicators under GLS, WLS, ULS, or DLS, the method statement of an invariance report had lost its sentence on the software and the estimator. Under all four, the reports of fit_solomon_sem_latent() and invariance_solomon() said that the CFI and RMSEA came from the unscaled maximum likelihood chi-square. With these estimators refused, neither can happen. A fit saved by an earlier version with another estimator is refused, with a message to fit it again. The report of fit_solomon_sem() now names the lavaan version and the estimator, and cites Yuan and Bentler (2000) under MLR, as the latent reports do; before, it gave an ML fit the same words as an MLR fit. fit_solomon_sem() stores the name in estimator; for a fit saved before, the report reads the estimator from lavaan’s options. The report needs the lavaan model in fit, from which it reads the version and the degrees of freedom and checks the estimator, so a result without it now stops with a message; the print and tidy() do not need it. With equal_var = TRUE, its method statement said that the four-group model is saturated, which it is not, since the constraint gives it 3 degrees of freedom; it now says that the posttest variances were constrained to be equal, and ?fit_solomon_sem says when the model is saturated.
  • Results are unchanged under "MLR" and "ML". With three and with four indicators, every number, table, print, and report sentence of fit_solomon_sem_latent() and invariance_solomon(), and every number, print, and result sentence of fit_solomon_sem(), equals that of the development version before this change under lavaan 0.7-3, as a test against stored results shows.
  • No validation script or article calls these functions with another estimator.

Covariates given as a vector or a matrix (bug fix, #146)

  • fit_solomon_glm(), with one treatment or several, left some forms of covariates out of the model without an error or a warning, so its results were those of a fit without them. The help named two forms, a data frame and, with data, the names of its columns. Before this change:

    • Without data, a vector, a matrix, or an array was left out.
    • With data, a vector given by its bare name (covariates = w) was used, whether or not it was a column of data, but a date-time of class POSIXlt and an array given by their bare names were left out.
    • With data, a matrix, such as cbind(age, w), and a vector given as an expression, such as age / 10 or d$age, were left out.
    • A vector or a one-dimensional array with names, such as participant ids or the clusters that name the values of tapply(age, cluster, mean)[as.character(cluster)], stopped instead with an unclear error, such as “object ‘id1’ not found”, because its names entered the model formula. With data, a vector with names given by its bare name was used.
    • A value of the wrong length stopped, as it still does.

  • In fit_solomon_glm() and check_solomon_missing(), every form is now used or stops with an error:

    • A numeric, logical, or factor vector is one covariate, with names or without. It is named by the variable when given by its bare name (covariates = age), as with data before, and covariate otherwise. A one-dimensional array without a class, such as tapply(age, cluster, mean)[as.character(cluster)] gives, is taken as a vector. One with a class, such as a table, stops with the advice to give c(covariates).
    • A numeric or logical matrix is one covariate per column, named by its column names, with covariate1, covariate2, … by position for columns without one. With data, a matrix column given by its bare name, such as d$age_z <- scale(d$age) makes, is named as glm() names it when it is given by its name: age_z when it has one column, and otherwise the name of the column followed by each column’s name, or by its position when it has no column names (two1, two2). The two calls give the same coefficients. The model data hold the matrix when it is given by its name, and its columns when it is given by its bare name, so with several columns the printed formulas differ. check_solomon_missing() still shows a matrix column of several columns, given by its name, as one table that pools its columns, as before (see its help). By its bare name, a numeric or logical one is shown by one table per column, and a character one stops (see below). A character matrix column of one column is one categorical covariate, named by the column, by its bare name as by its name. cbind() turns a factor into its integer codes, and with a character vector makes every column character, which stops, so such covariates go in a data frame, such as data.frame(age, region).
    • A data frame or a matrix with two columns of the same name stops, and so does a data frame with a column without a name.
    • Any other form stops with an error that says what to give instead. Examples are a character vector without data (names of columns need data, and a categorical covariate goes in as a factor), a list that is not a data frame, an array of more than two dimensions, and a vector of another type, such as a date (it goes in as a column of a data frame).
    • When covariates alone has the wrong length, the error now says that it takes one value or one row per participant.

  • With data, names in covariates that are not columns of data stop with an error that lists them. Before, such names stopped with “Inputs must have the same length”, which did not say why. A character vector with one value per participant, given as an expression, such as ifelse(age > 40, "old", "young"), was left out instead; it now stops with that error, which says that a categorical covariate goes in as a factor. A name given twice stops too; before, fit_solomon_glm() stopped because the two copies were collinear, and check_solomon_missing() gave no gap.

  • Forms that gave a fit before and now stop. With data, a vector from outside data given by its bare name is now used only when it is numeric, logical, or a factor, as without data. Before, it entered the model as it was, whatever its type, but for a POSIXlt date-time, which was left out. A character vector, which was a categorical covariate, is now read as names of columns, so it stops with the error above. A date (Date), a date-time (POSIXct), or a time difference (difftime) stops too. Give any of them as a column of a data frame, or of data: a vector column of data given by its bare name is used whatever its atomic type, as before. A one-dimensional array without a class, a numeric or logical matrix, and a POSIXlt date-time, which were left out, are now used too.

  • Data frames whose columns lack names of their own now stop. Before:

    • with two columns of the same name, fit_solomon_glm() used only the first, and check_solomon_missing() showed the first twice and left the second out of its fit;
    • a data frame without names was left out of both;
    • a column named "" stopped fit_solomon_glm() with “attempt to use zero-length variable name”, and check_solomon_missing() gave it an empty table and gave no gap;
    • a column named NA was used by fit_solomon_glm(), but check_solomon_missing() gave it an empty table.

  • A covariate named as a column of the model now stops check_solomon_missing() when y_pre is numeric, with the error that fit_solomon_glm() gives (“Rename these covariates, whose names the model uses: y.”). The names are y, pretested, pre_obs, log_exposure, and treat or, with several treatments, condition and treat_ followed by each treatment’s name. Before, a data frame with such a column stopped the fit behind the gap and the delta line, and check_solomon_missing() left both out without a word. A vector now takes its bare name, so covariates = y stops too; before, it was named covariates. Without y_pre there is no such fit, and a covariate of any name is shown by its loss.

  • A logical or character matrix column of several columns now stops when given by its name or in a data frame, such as covariates = "lm2" with d$lm2 <- cbind(d$age > 40, d$z > 0), with an error that says to give its columns as columns of a data frame or, for a logical one, the column by its bare name, which takes one covariate per column. Before, fit_solomon_glm() stopped in glm() with an unclear error (“replacement has 240 rows, data has 120”, for 120 participants and two columns), and check_solomon_missing() with numeric y_pre left out the gap and the delta line without a word; it now stops with the fit’s error. Without y_pre, such a column is shown as one table, as before. Given by its bare name, a character one now stops too, in both functions and with or without y_pre. Before, fit_solomon_glm() left it out, and check_solomon_missing() did not stop: it showed one table per column, named by the matrix’s column names (V1, V2, … by position for columns without one), and with numeric y_pre took the gap and the delta line from a fit that included those columns, unlike fit_solomon_glm().

  • check_solomon_missing() converted other forms with as.data.frame(): a vector was named covariates, the columns of a matrix without names V1, V2, …, and a list or a character vector was accepted. They are now named, or refused, as in fit_solomon_glm().

  • Results are unchanged for every other form that the help named, and for a numeric, logical, or factor vector given by its bare name with data. In a comparison of 88 results made for this change, the values, names, classes, attributes, and printed output are identical to those of the development version before it: fits with one and with several treatments, with covariates given as data frames, tibbles, data frames with row names, names of columns, bare column names, and vectors outside data by their bare names, with model-based, HC3, and CR2 covariances, binary and count outcomes, both pretest centers, and missing posttests; their prints, summaries, tidy(), and reports; perm_solomon(), marginal_solomon(), plot_sensitization(), and equivalence_solomon() of them; and check_solomon_missing() and validate_solomon(). A test stores 18 such results from that version, 14 fits and 4 check_solomon_missing() results. It compares the formulas, coefficient names, and classes exactly; the model data and the tables exactly but for their doubles, which it compares to 1e-12 of their value, as their last bits depend on the platform; and the effects, coefficients, gaps, and deltas to 1e-8.

  • perm_solomon(), marginal_solomon(), and plot_sensitization() work from the data stored in the fit, and report_solomon(), equivalence_solomon(), tidy(), and glance() from its results, so a vector or a matrix gives them the same results as the equivalent data frame. Tests check this for each.

Covariates far from zero (bug fix, #137)

  • fit_solomon_glm() stopped with “system is computationally singular” when a covariate lay far from zero relative to its spread, as a calendar year, an identification number, or a score with a large offset can, or was on a scale far from 1, as an income in dollars can: in the issue’s example, a covariate with a mean of 10,000 and a standard deviation of 1. The influence functions of the pretest effects, added in #104, inverted the cross-products of the design, which square its condition number; they now come from the model’s QR decomposition. Short of that error, the HC3 and CR2 standard errors and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, the delta method and the bootstrap of marginal_solomon(), and the intervals of the cell means of plot_sensitization() lost accuracy, without a warning. At a mean of 1,000 standard deviations the delta-method standard errors of marginal_solomon() for counts were off by up to 4e-3 of their value, and from 10,000 every bootstrap resample failed.
  • A pretest on a scale far from 1 did the same. With a pretest standard deviation of 10^-8 or 10^8, HC3 and CR2 fits stopped with the same error. Short of that, the CR2 standard errors were off, in three checks, by 3.5e-6 to 5.8e-6 of their value at a standard deviation of 10^6 and by 1.2e-3 to 5.5e-3 at 10^7; in one check, the delta-method standard errors of marginal_solomon(), whose numerical derivatives took steps unsuited to the pretest’s coefficient, were off by 3e-7 to 4e-7 of their value at 10^4 and by 2e-3 to 3e-3 at 10^6.
  • The inference is now computed with each numeric covariate standardized, centered at its mean and divided by its standard deviation over the participants in the model, and with the pretest, centered already, divided by the power of two nearest its standard deviation. That is a reparameterization of the same model, so adding a constant to a covariate or to the pretest, or changing the scale of either, changes no contrast, standard error, degrees of freedom, or p-value beyond rounding, for constants up to at least 10^6 standard deviations: under model-based, HC3, and CR2 covariance, with one or several treatments, at either pretest center, and in marginal_solomon(), plot_sensitization(), and perm_solomon(). The model, the coefficients (the intercept included), and their covariance are still those of the covariates and the pretest as given; the standardized ones are in a new element, covariate_scaling, outside the stable interface. A numeric covariate is standardized whatever its class, such as a labeled column read from SPSS or one wrapped in I(), and dates and times as the numbers they enter the model as. The warnings, theta, and dispersion come from the standardized fit: far from zero, the negative-binomial fit to the covariates as given could warn that theta did not converge where the same model standardized converged. ?fit_solomon_glm has a new section, “Covariates”.
  • Exactly collinear covariates far from zero, such as z + 1e6 and 2 * z + 3, whose rounding error makes glm() take them for distinct covariates, were fitted under model-based covariance, with meaningless coefficients for the two, and stopped under HC3 and CR2 with “system is computationally singular”. The standardized model is now checked for collinear terms too: each term, regressed on the terms before it, is taken to be collinear when its residual is within 4 times the rounding error that the regression carries into it, or within the 1e-11 of glm(). That error is the term’s own plus each other term’s times the magnitude of its coefficient, with each value’s error taken to be .Machine$double.eps times its magnitude as given; the residual is computed from the stored values in twice the working precision, rather than taken from the QR decomposition, whose rounding the same coefficients would multiply. So it covers a term whose spread is small next to that of the far terms it is a combination of, such as a delay that is the difference of two dates, and a term that is the small difference of two nearly equal ones. An exact relation among the covariates, the pretest, the treatment and pretest indicators, their interaction, and factor indicators therefore stops with the message that names a collinear term, as it does near zero, however far from zero its terms lie and however their spreads differ, as long as its values carry no more rounding error than values stored from exact data or computed in a few operations. A term that is not exactly collinear stops only when its residual is within that bound or below the tolerance of glm(). Near zero the bound grows with the term’s coefficients. For a covariate that nearly repeats another, such as a covariate and its copy in single precision, it is about 5e-15 of the covariate’s norm, far below that tolerance, so the check is that of glm() and such covariates are fitted as before, whatever other covariates lie far from zero. It exceeds that tolerance once the magnitudes of the coefficients sum to more than about 4,000, as in nested near-collinearity: with z2 = z1 + 1e-6 * e1 and z3 = e1 + delta * e2, the fit goes ahead at delta = 1e-8 and stops at delta = 3e-9 and below, where glm() still fits the model, because such a residual cannot be told from that of an exact relation between rounded values. A fit of the model as given that fails itself stops before the check, as before: MASS::glm.nb() did, with “NA/NaN/Inf in ‘x’”, for an exact relation with a covariate 3 * 10^10 standard deviations from zero.
  • fit_solomon_sem(ancova = TRUE) lost accuracy when the pretest lay far from zero: at 10^4 standard deviations its p-values were off by 7% to 100% of their value in six checks, and in another it stopped, as it did from 10^6 in every check, where compare_solomon_methods() then left out its SEM ANCOVA row; the latent ANCOVA of fit_solomon_sem_latent() lost accuracy too. Both now center the pretest, or its items, at the mean among the pretested participants, which changes only intercepts and means: the intercepts of the lavaan model of the observed ANCOVA are now the posttest means adjusted to that pretest. check_solomon_assumptions() centers the pretest in its test of homogeneous slopes, which was NA, or wrong, from a pretest mean of 10^7 standard deviations.
  • fit_solomon_mi() stopped in the same way when the pretest lay far from zero, or was on a scale far from 1, with a standard deviation of about 1e-8 or 1e7 in one check. With posttests missing in a pretested group, the results of a seed also changed by Monte Carlo error when a constant was added to the pretest, even one standard deviation, and from a pretest mean of about 10^7 standard deviations the imputation models took the pretest to be constant and stopped. Its analysis of the completed data sets now centers the pretest and divides it by the power of two nearest its standard deviation, as fit_solomon_glm() does, and its imputation models center it at its mean among each pretested group’s observed posttests, so the results of fit_solomon_mi() and tipping_point_solomon() no longer depend on where the pretest lies or on its scale. The imputations have the same distribution as before, but those of a given seed differ, so results with a seed change by Monte Carlo error.
  • What changes on ordinary data. Dividing the pretest by a power of two is exact, so fits with a pretest and no numeric covariate agree with the development version before this change within about 2e-11 of their value, except the delta-method standard errors of marginal_solomon(), which move by about 1e-9. With covariates of modest magnitude and location, results agree with it to about 1e-8 of their value, as a test against results stored from it shows, for every family and covariance, with missing posttests and clusters; the delta-method standard errors of marginal_solomon() move by about that much, because the delta method now takes the exact derivatives of the contrasts rather than numerical ones, whose error that was, and negative-binomial results by the convergence tolerance of theta, about 1e-9. With a covariate on a large scale, such as an income in dollars, or far from zero, such as a calendar year or a date, the previous CR2 and delta-method results were off by up to about 5e-5 of their value, and the delta-method standard errors by about 3e-3 for a covariate with a standard deviation of 10^6; the corrected values can change the last printed digit of an interval or a p-value. Fits whose covariates are on scales far from 1, which stopped under HC3 and CR2, now succeed. The contrasts of the SEM ANCOVA move by the convergence tolerance of lavaan’s optimization, about 1e-7 of their value, and their p-values by up to about 5e-6 of theirs.
  • Other changes. With a pretest or a numeric covariate, fit_solomon_glm() fits the model twice, as given and standardized. Under CR2 with a pretest or a numeric covariate, vcov is now a plain matrix rather than the clubSandwich object, whose small-sample adjustments belong to the standardized model: it is still what ?fit_solomon_glm documents, the covariance matrix of the coefficients, but code that passes it to clubSandwich with model now stops. As said above, the imputations of fit_solomon_mi() for a given seed differ from those of earlier versions, with the same distribution. A difference between a contrast’s estimates at the two pretest centers that is zero but for rounding error, such as that of a rate ratio, which does not depend on the center, is printed without the sign of that error.
  • A numeric covariate whose name another column of the model shares, such as a covariate wave2 beside a factor wave, whose second level’s indicator is also named wave2, or flagTRUE beside a logical flag. The standardized covariates were found by name, so the indicator was rescaled in place of the covariate, and the estimates and standard errors of the intercept and the covariates, the cells of plot_sensitization(), and the marginal contrasts at the observed center were wrong, without a warning. The covariates are now found by their position in the model. Earlier versions also gave the second of the two columns the standard error of the first and left it out of the cells of plot_sensitization(), and CR2 fits stopped with “duplicate ‘row.names’ are not allowed”; such fits now give the results of the same model with the covariate renamed. plot_sensitization() also took a covariate named pre_obs, in a fit without a pretest, for the pretest; it is now a covariate like any other.
  • Nearly collinear covariates, about 10^-7 of their standard deviation apart or closer. sandwich::vcovHC() and clubSandwich::vcovCR() form the HC3 and CR2 covariances from the inverse of X'WX, whose condition number is the square of the design’s, so their standard errors lost accuracy, by 2% and 3% for a covariate near zero and its copy in single precision in one check, and from about 10^-8 apart near zero HC3 and CR2 fits stopped with “system is computationally singular”. With a numeric covariate they are now computed from the QR decomposition of the standardized model: HC3 from the participants’ influences, and CR2 by clubSandwich in an orthonormal basis of the same columns, which gives the same covariance, Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, and Wald tests. With covariates 10^-8 standard deviations apart near zero, the standard errors and degrees of freedom of the contrasts and the coefficients and the statistics of the omnibus tests of several treatments agreed with those of an exact reparameterization to about 2e-8 of their value under every covariance, in a battery of 708 cases, and their p-values to about 1e-6; at 10^-9, to about 2e-7 and 3e-6; and the standard errors of the contrasts to about 1e-6 at 10^-10 under HC3 and CR2. The studentized statistic of perm_solomon() uses the HC3 variance computed the same way. Fits without a numeric covariate keep the computations of sandwich and clubSandwich, and their results.
  • With such covariates the delta method of marginal_solomon() was wrong too. For a covariate near zero and its copy in single precision, its standard errors under model-based covariance were up to 45 times too large: its numerical derivatives took steps of 1e-6 times each coefficient, too large for the large coefficients of nearly collinear covariates, and the variance of its linear approximation, formed from the covariance, canceled the large entries of the covariance. Its bootstrap, which solved the normal equations, failed in every resample. The delta method now takes the exact derivatives of the contrasts and computes their variance through the QR decomposition, or in the orthonormal basis under CR2, and the bootstrap refits by QR. For that copy, the delta method’s results agree with those of the exact reparameterization to about 2e-8 of their value under every covariance, and the bootstrap’s standard errors to 1e-9.
  • Not changed here: glm() takes nearly collinear covariates as given to be collinear, which stops the fit, when they lie so far from zero that their difference falls below about 1e-11 of their distance from zero, as for covariates 10^-6 standard deviations apart at 10^6 standard deviations from zero; and the ties of perm_solomon() with models fitted by iteration, and the first stage of its clustered test, which is fitted to the covariates as given, remain on #134.

broom and dplyr are no longer imported (#84, fourth part)

  • solomonR no longer imports broom and dplyr, which brought in 8 of the 36 packages that it needed, directly or through other packages (backports, broom, dplyr, purrr, stringi, stringr, tidyr, and tidyselect). None of the 28 that remain needs either one. The coefficient tables of fit_solomon_glm() and the legacy ancova and t_unpretested tables of fit_solomon_classic() are now made with base R and tibble. tibble is now required at version 3.2.0 or later, the version that dplyr required.
  • dplyr is now suggested, for the deprecated plot_solomon() alone. Where dplyr is installed, plot_solomon() makes its cell summaries with dplyr, as before, and so loads it, and dplyr’s methods keep the groups of the returned table up to date when the table is changed. Where dplyr is not installed, base R and tibble make the same table.
  • Results are unchanged. For 1,383 results of the exported functions and of the examples of every help page, with their prints, summaries, tidy(), glance(), reports, and plot data, the values, names, column order, classes, attributes, row names, and printed output are identical to those of the development version before this change, except as the next item says, and so is what the smoke run of the binary-outcome validation script writes. The tests pass where neither package is installed.
  • What depended on the package loading broom and dplyr.
    • tidy() and glance() of a model that a result holds, such as fit$model of fit_solomon_glm() or fit$tests$E$model of fit_solomon_classic(), need broom loaded, as they do for any model fitted outside the package; before, the first fit of a session had loaded broom. broom also has a tidy() method for NULL, so tidy(fit$model) of a classic fit, whose model is NULL (its models are fit$tests$E$model and fit$tests$H$model), returned an empty table, and it now fails unless broom is loaded.
    • Unless broom is loaded, tidy() or glance() of a result that has no such method fails with the error of generics, “no applicable method for ‘glance’ applied to an object of class …”, instead of broom’s, “No glance() method for objects of class …”. This is glance() of every result except those of fit_solomon_glm(), and tidy() of the results that have no table of effects, such as equivalence and permutation tests, checks, and reports.
    • Where dplyr is not installed, the table that plot_solomon() returns prints without its # Groups: pretested [2] line, and base R and tibble do not maintain its groups: as.data.frame() keeps its groups attribute, and taking rows of it or changing its pretested column leaves the groups as they were, so a table changed in that way gives wrong groups if it is later used with dplyr. Scores that are not numbers, which plot_solomon() does not accept by its documentation, give R’s own warnings and errors, cell by cell, instead of the single warning or error of dplyr that wrapped them, and the message that dplyr gives under options(dplyr.summarise.inform = TRUE) is not given.
  • The first fit of a session is faster, because it loads 6 packages instead of 14. In new R sessions, the first call of fit_solomon_classic() on solomon_example took a median of 0.53 s before this change and 0.23 s after (8 sessions each, alternating, with R 4.6.1 on Windows and the packages’ files in the disk cache); later calls take 0.05 s or less either way.
  • The binary-outcome validation script binds its rows without dplyr, and stops on tables that it could not bind as dplyr::bind_rows() did; a test builds its stored table without broom. Every validation script passes in smoke mode without either package.
  • The tests need testthat 3.1.7 or later, for with_mocked_bindings(), and DESCRIPTION now says so; the minimum it declared, 3.0.0, was already too low for expect_no_warning(), which came in 3.1.5.

The a priori procedure in the planning article (#147)

  • “Planning a Solomon Study” gains a short section, “Planning for precision”, on the a priori procedure (APP) of Trafimow (2017): a sample size chosen for how close an estimate will be to its parameter, and with what probability, rather than for power. The package does not implement it; the proposal is #147, on the Post-1.0 milestone with #118. The article’s four sources are added to the references.

The pretest center when posttests are missing (#135)

With a pretest covariate, the pretest effects compare the pretested groups, at a mean pretest, with the unpretested groups. When posttests are missing, that mean can be taken over the pretested participants analyzed or over every observed pretest, and the pretest effects differ by the pretest slope times the difference between the two means. The data cannot tell which is right, and no published source decides; the choice and its reasons are set out in the decision record posted on #135.

  • The default is unchanged. The pretest effects are still evaluated at the mean pretest of the pretested participants in the model, pretest_center = "analyzed". It assumes that, within each treatment condition, the pretested and the unpretested groups lost the same kinds of participants. The record keeps it because, when taking the pretest changes neither the posttest nor who stays, random assignment makes every group lose alike and its test of a zero pretest effect keeps its level, while the other center’s rejected in 54% of data sets in the record’s check (500 data sets of 200 per group, a third of the posttests lost by baseline in all four groups); it fails only when taking the pretest changed who stayed. Every number that a fit, a report, or a print gave before is unchanged with the default, as a test against results stored from the development version before this change shows; the new lines and the behavior changes below are the exceptions.
  • pretest_center = "observed" in fit_solomon_glm() (one or several treatments), fit_solomon_mmrm(), fit_solomon_1949(), and marginal_solomon() evaluates them at the mean of every observed pretest among the pretested participants, with or without a posttest; the rows of the participants without a posttest must be in the data. It assumes that the pretested groups’ losses depend at most on the observed pretest, and that the unpretested groups’ losses are unrelated to baseline as well as to the posttest. Its standard errors take the variance of that mean over every participant who contributes to it, in the model or not, by stacking its estimating equation with the model’s (Stefanski & Boos, 2002), under model-based, HC3, and CR2 covariance; a CR2 fit needs the cluster of every such participant. The treatment contrasts, Pretest x Treatment, and the fitted values do not depend on the center. On the risk and rate scales of marginal_solomon(), the center also moves Treatment | pretested, the average treatment effect, and Pretest x Treatment.
  • Both centers are returned and printed. Fits with a pretest covariate return pretest_center, pretest_mean_analyzed, pretest_mean_observed, pretest_n, and pretest_sensitivity, the pretest effects at both centers with their difference, the attrition of each group, and, on the identity link, the delta line: for each unpretested group, the offset between its dropouts’ and its completers’ mean posttest that the default assumes (National Research Council, 2010, pp. 88–89; Mavridis et al., 2015, sec. 2). Whenever the two centers differ, the printed fit gives them in a block, as the record’s section 4 shows it for mai2020, and report_solomon() names the center used, its assumption, and the other center, and says when whether a pretest effect differs from zero depends on the center, or, when only its sign differs, its direction. The caption of plot_sensitization() names both centers. marginal_solomon() prints the contrasts that move under both standardizations, and fit_solomon_1949() both inferred pretests. These tables are outside the output contract of ?solomon_output for now.
  • New lines whenever a posttest is missing. The print methods and report_solomon() of the fits, marginal_solomon(), and fit_solomon_1949() give the share of posttests missing among the pretested and the unpretested participants, with the range over the groups, whether or not the centers differ.
  • check_solomon_missing() gains covariates and the record’s attrition checks: the share missing by group, between the pretest conditions and between the conditions (What Works Clearinghouse, 2022, p. 40), with a statement when Fisher’s exact test of loss by pretest condition gives p < .05; the pretest scores of those lost (Campbell, 1957, pp. 301–302); each pretested condition’s selection shift, with its standard error and a Wald test of equal shifts, and the raw comparison of posttest means when that test gives p < .05 (#143); the gap between the centers (What Works Clearinghouse, 2022, Equation H.2, p. 207) and the delta line; loss by each covariate within each pretest condition (Lee, 2005, Remark 4, p. 16; Groenwold et al., 2014), by Fisher’s exact test for two levels and a simulated p-value for more; the pretested participants with a posttest and no pretest (#142); and what cannot be checked (Campbell, 1957, p. 305). validate_solomon() leaves these checks out. Its guidance now says that complete-case analysis is unbiased under its condition for the treatment contrasts only.
  • analysis_plan_solomon() gains pretest_center. Its population, missing-at-random, and multiple-imputation statements are restricted to the treatment contrasts, and a new item states the population, the assumption, and the center of the pretest effects. A plan that assumes missingness at random for the pretest effects chooses "observed".
  • Behavior changes. A four-group fit with an empty group, or a term collinear with the others, now stops with an error that names the groups, as fits with several treatments did; before, it returned NA estimates or failed in the linear algebra. With HC3, a four-group fit with a group of one participant now stops with an error that names it, as fits with several treatments did; before, it returned NaN standard errors, or, with a pretest covariate, failed with an unclear error. fit_solomon_mmrm() takes a participant’s pretest from any of the participant’s rows, so a pretest given on one row only no longer excludes the participant with a warning; different pretests for one participant still stop the fit.
  • Help pages. ?fit_solomon_glm has a new section, “The pretest effect when posttests are missing”. ?fit_solomon_ml says that its fit, which needs every posttest, has one center, and that removing the participants without a posttest gives the default’s. ?fit_solomon_mi and ?tipping_point_solomon say that their imputations embody the observed center in the pretested groups. ?equivalence_solomon says that equivalence of a pretest effect holds only under its center’s assumption. ?fit_solomon_mmrm says that later-occasion pretest effects are biased at either center when dropout depends on baseline beyond the earlier posttests. The article “Missing and Repeated Posttests” shows both centers on data of each one’s case.
  • Citations corrected. The premise that random assignment makes the unpretested groups’ expected pretest equal to the pretested groups’ is now credited to Solomon (1949, p. 141), and the pooled mean as its best estimate to Solomon and Lessac (1968, p. 147), in ?fit_solomon_glm, ?marginal_solomon, “Getting Started”, “Solomon Methods”, the teaching article, and the news of #104; they had been credited to Solomon and Lessac (1968, pp. 146–147).
  • Not solved here. Pretested participants without a pretest are dropped at either center (#142), and when the treatment conditions lose different kinds of participants neither center gives both conditional pretest effects, and Pretest x Treatment is biased at every center (#143). check_solomon_missing() reports both cases.
  • tools/pretest-center-check.R reruns the record’s checks with both centers, from one build of the package.

Validation scripts outside a git clone (bug fix, #152)

  • Ten validation scripts stopped at the end of a run, before writing their run-information file, when they ran outside any git repository, as in a copy downloaded with GitHub’s “Download ZIP” and unpacked outside one: the scripts of the binary, historical-test, cluster-marginal, cluster, count, negative-binomial, invariance, multiple-imputation, repeated-measures, and several-treatment studies. The file is run-information.csv, or nb-run-information.csv for the negative-binomial study. The scripts took the commit from git rev-parse HEAD. Outside a repository, git fails, and R’s system() returns an empty character vector, character(0), with a warning that the scripts’ tryCatch() did not catch, so there was no commit to record, not even NA. In such a copy, tools/check-validation-scripts.R failed these ten and the two scripts that depend on them, 12 of the 16. In a copy unpacked inside another git repository, git finds that repository, and the ten recorded its commit.
  • Every validation script that records a commit now takes it by one rule: the environment variable SOLOMONR_COMMIT when it is set and not empty; otherwise the commit checked out, when git is on the PATH, the copy is the top level of a git repository, git agrees to read that repository, and its DESCRIPTION names solomonR; otherwise NA. A run from a clone that git refuses to read, as by default it refuses one owned by another user unless git’s safe.directory setting lists it, records NA; the scripts leave that setting as it is. The copy is the package that the script loads, found as pkgload::load_all() finds it, and git looks for the repository from the copy alone, whatever GIT_DIR and GIT_WORK_TREE say. The scripts of the ML, power, and plan re-simulation studies, which read only SOLOMONR_COMMIT, now also record the commit of a clone. The rule does not detect uncommitted changes: a run from a clone with changes records the commit checked out, which does not contain them. Such a run should set SOLOMONR_COMMIT to the commit and a description of the changes, as the stored runs of the ML and power studies did. Without it, these three scripts recorded NA for such a run, and now record the commit checked out. The Validation Evidence page states the rule, says where the commit of a downloaded copy is stored and how to record it, and says under “Adding a study” how a new study’s script takes up the rule. The stored results do not change.
  • The several-treatment script, rerun where the old script stopped outside any git repository, resumes from the checkpoints that it left, whose commit is empty, and records NA as the commit of their replications.
  • A new test checks that the scripts share one definition of the rule and pass it the folder of the package that they load. It checks the rule with SOLOMONR_COMMIT set; in a clone, also from a folder below its root and with uncommitted changes; outside any repository; inside an unrelated repository; in a repository without commits; in a clone that git refuses to read; and with GIT_DIR or GIT_WORK_TREE pointing at another repository. It also checks that the messages that git prints are discarded, that a ZIP or tar file made by git archive stores its commit where the page says, and that every study whose script has the definition, including one added later, has an article, named after its folder, that links the rule.
  • The validation-scripts workflow now also runs the plan re-simulation script in smoke mode from a copy made with git archive, outside any git repository, and fails unless the run records NA as its commit. A run of a script, not only the rule itself, is now tested on every pull request to master and every push to it (#162).
  • The same workflow now runs tests/testthat/test-validation-commit.R from the package source. All its tests read vignettes/articles/: they load validation_commit() from a script, and some also check the Validation Evidence page. R CMD check and the coverage workflow do not have that folder, so until now the whole file was skipped on every CI run and ran only locally (#162).
  • GitHub makes the “Download ZIP” file, and its other source archives of a branch, tag, or commit, with git archive (GitHub, n.d.). GitHub’s page does not say whether these files keep the commit. On November 7, 2026, they did: unzip -z printed the commit from GitHub’s ZIP file of master and from its ZIP file of the tag v0.4.0, and git get-tar-commit-id printed it from its .tar.gz file of master. The Validation Evidence page now says so, citing Git’s documentation (Git Project, n.d.) for where git archive stores the commit. Both are added to the references (#162).

References without a date (#162)

  • tools/check-references.R now also checks references without a date (“n.d.”), which it skipped before: the first two, GitHub (n.d.) and Git Project (n.d.), came with #162. It also orders names as APA 7 does, letter by letter, with the end of a surname or of a set of initials before any letter, so “Brown, J.” precedes “Browning, A.”; before, the check would have accepted the reverse. Accented letters count as their base letters, so “Éthier” sorts under E. No list in the package changes its verdict.

Validation scripts that run against the current package (#140)

  • The simulation scripts behind the validation articles select the rows they study by label, as ?solomon_output describes, so they run against the current package again. Several took the rows of an effects table by position, and the pretest effects added in #104 broke them: the scripts of the binary, count, negative-binomial, and repeated-measures studies ran to the end but caught an error in their replications and reported no usable one, the multiple-imputation script stopped, the cluster-marginal script stored values under the wrong labels, and the agreement check of the study with several treatments compared the wrong rows. A row that a script does not find by its label now stops the study.
  • Two quantities had changed meaning with the package, and the scripts now compute them as the runs did. The cluster-marginal script counts degrees of freedom below 4 in the rows it studies, because the warning it counted has also covered the pretest effects since #104. The replication of the historical tests reads the one-tailed p of Test I from p_one_tailed, because p.value has been the two-tailed p since Test I was judged by it after #51.
  • What the scripts compute is unchanged. On two replications of the scenarios of the smoke mode described below, the original and the adapted scripts give identical results with the package at the commit of each study’s stored results, for the binary, cluster-marginal, cluster, count, negative-binomial, multiple-imputation, repeated-measures, and several-treatment studies and the re-simulation of plan_solomon(). The original scripts of the historical tests and of the invariance study, at the commits of their runs, and the adapted scripts, with the current package, give identical results too. The runs of the ML and power studies used versions of the package that were not committed, so their scripts were checked at nearby commits. With the current package, pretest-adjusted results differ from those at the commits of the runs, with relative differences below 1e-7, because the pretest has been centered since #104, and the Test I rows of the power study differ, because power_solomon() has judged Test I by the two-tailed p since the decision after #51. Each article says what was checked. The stored results, and so the articles’ numbers, do not change.
  • Every validation script has a smoke mode. With the environment variable SOLOMONR_SMOKE_DIR set, it runs SOLOMONR_SMOKE_REPS replications (default 2) of a few scenarios, writes everything under that folder, and stops if a replication caught an error or gave no usable result. tools/check-validation-scripts.R runs every script in a -validation folder of the articles, at any depth, that way, and fails if one fails, has no smoke mode, or runs longer than SOLOMONR_SMOKE_TIMEOUT seconds, or if a file of the package changes. A new GitHub Actions workflow runs it on pushes and pull requests to master; its first run, on #144, passed. The check is not part of R CMD check.
  • The confirmatory studies of the multiple-imputation (#82) and repeated-measures (#57) functions, planned under #117, will be reported in their articles beside the first studies, with their own scripts. The first studies and their verdicts stay as reported.

One output vocabulary (#110)

The names that results use are settled before 1.0, as #83 settled the names of the arguments. Code that reads results by a former label or element name needs the new one. Former element names keep working with $ through v1.x, with a deprecation warning. The stable parts of a result are the effects table, conf_level, and tidy(), and the new help page ?solomon_output states the contract. Each item below that can break existing code says what that code needs.

  • Contrast labels that can break code. fit_solomon_sem() and fit_solomon_sem_latent() label their contrasts as every other fit does: ATE (avg over pretest) (was ATE), Pretest x Treatment (was Sens), Treatment | pretested (was Pre_Eff), and Treatment | unpretested (was Unpre_Eff). Their ANCOVA models of the pretested groups label their one contrast Treatment | pretested. Code that selects rows by a former label, such as effects$contrast == "Sens", needs the new label. plot_solomon_effects(), report_solomon(), and compare_solomon_methods() no longer translate the labels. A SEM fit saved by an earlier version keeps its former labels, so tidy(), report_solomon(), and plot_solomon_effects() stop for it and ask for it to be fitted again. Its print method shows it as it was stored.
  • New rows in the SEM effects tables. The four-group models of fit_solomon_sem() and fit_solomon_sem_latent() report the three pretest effects after the four treatment contrasts, as pretested minus unpretested participants: Pretest effect | control, Pretest effect | treated, and Pretest main effect. Code that takes rows by position, or expects four rows, should select them by label.
    • In the observed model their estimates equal those of fit_solomon_glm() without a pretest score; the standard errors and the tests are lavaan’s, with a normal reference distribution.
    • In the latent model they are differences between latent means, in the unit of the other contrasts. The pretest main effect is the effect Dukes et al. (1995, p. 426) describe, one of the four elements of their analyses planned under #117; the other three remain planned. A shift in an indicator’s intercept that the two pretested groups share biases the latent pretest effects, although it cancels from the Pretest x Treatment contrast.
    • The ANCOVA models use the pretested groups alone and report no pretest effects.
    The printed tables and report_solomon() give the new rows as they do for fit_solomon_glm(). plot_solomon_effects() and compare_solomon_methods() show the four treatment contrasts, as before.
  • Renamed elements. The table of contrasts is effects in every fit that has one:
    • fit_solomon_sem_latent(): effects_post is now effects, and fit_post is now fit, as in fit_solomon_sem(). conf_level is now at the top level, as in every other fit, and still in settings.
    • solomon_from_summary(): contrasts is now effects, for four-group designs and for designs with several treatments.
    The former names still work with $, as in fit$effects_post, and give a deprecation warning that names the new element. Only the whole former name is recognized, and [[ is not covered: fit[["effects_post"]] is NULL. A fit saved by an earlier version still gives its elements under the new names, as they were stored. A saved SEM fit has the former contrast labels as well, so tidy(), report_solomon(), and plot_solomon_effects() stop for it and ask for it to be fitted again.
  • fit_solomon_classic() returns conf_level at the top level too; it remains in settings.
  • One order of columns, which can break code that reads columns by position. Every effects table has the columns contrast, estimate, std.error, statistic, df, p.value, conf.low, and conf.high, in that order. The columns that index its rows come before them, and the columns of one class after them. Code that reads columns by name is not affected. What moved, and what is new:
    • fit_solomon_glm(), fit_solomon_ml(), and fit_solomon_mi(): df now precedes p.value, in effects and in the coefficients tables of the first two.
    • Designs with several treatments, in fit_solomon_glm() and solomon_from_summary(): df precedes p.value, and p.adjusted follows conf.high.
    • fit_solomon_mmrm(): statistic precedes df.
    • marginal_solomon(): std.error follows estimate, the interval follows p.value, and a new column, statistic, holds the test statistic. It is on the scale of the test, so for a ratio it is the log of the estimate divided by std.error.
    • fit_solomon_sem() and fit_solomon_sem_latent(): a new column, df, after statistic.
    • compare_solomon_methods()$results: method comes first, then the shared columns, with a new statistic, and then adjustment, variance, and reference.
    • tipping_point_solomon()$results: new columns contrast and statistic, after the offsets delta and delta_sd.
    • fit_solomon_classic(): the result of each of Tests A-H, and pretest_main, have a new contrast column and F after the interval. The test column of pretest_main is now empty, and its label is in contrast.
    • baseline_solomon(), which compares pretests and has no effects table, lists its test before its interval too: statistic, df, and p.value precede conf.low and conf.high.
  • df is in every effects table. Where the test uses the normal distribution it is Inf, not NA, as fit_solomon_glm() already reported for binomial and Poisson fits. That is so in the SEM fits, whose tables had no df, in fit_solomon_ml() with inference = "wald", and in marginal_solomon() without CR2 covariance. Every p-value is then 2 * pt(-abs(statistic), df), and equivalence_solomon(), plot_solomon_effects(), and report_solomon() read Inf as the normal reference.
  • fit_solomon_classic() has an effects table, as every other fit does: Tests A-H and the pretest main effect, one row each, in the shared columns, with the test letter in test and F last. The contrasts have the shared labels: Pretest x Treatment (Test A), Treatment | pretested (Tests B, E, F, and G), Treatment | unpretested (Tests C and H), ATE (avg over pretest) (Test D), and Pretest main effect. The tests element is unchanged apart from the columns of each result.
  • fit_solomon_classic()$aov is replaced by $anova, which can change results with unequal group sizes. anova is the two-by-two analysis of variance of the posttest with Type III sums of squares, in the format of solomon_from_summary()$anova: sources Treatment, Pretest, Pretest x Treatment, and Error, and columns source, sumsq, df, meansq, F, and p.value. Its F tests are the squares of the t tests of Test D, the pretest main effect, and Test A, and the table equals the one solomon_from_summary() gives for the same cells.
    • aov held the sequential sums of squares of stats::aov(): treatment ignoring pretesting, then pretesting adjusted for treatment, then the interaction. With unequal group sizes its treatment row was not Test D and its pretest row was not the pretest main effect; only its interaction row agreed with Test A. With equal group sizes the two tables have the same sums of squares.
    • $aov still works, with a deprecation warning that says so, and returns anova: the columns are no longer those of broom::tidy() (term, df, sumsq, meansq, statistic, p.value), and the last row is Error, not Residuals. [["aov"]] is NULL. A fit saved by an earlier version has no anova table, and $aov gives NULL for it; refit it.
    • The elements ancova, t_unpretested, and stouffer stay as legacy elements outside the stable interface; Tests E, H, and I hold the same analyses.
  • A renamed ANOVA source. In the four-group table solomon_from_summary()$anova, the interaction is Pretest x Treatment, as the contrast is named; it was Treatment x Pretest. Code that selects that row by name needs the new name. The table for designs with several treatments already had Pretest x Condition. The conclusion that fit_solomon_classic() gives when Test A is significant and neither simple effect is says “Pretest x Treatment interaction” as well. A four-group solomon_from_summary() result saved by an earlier version keeps the former name, and report_solomon() stops for it and asks for the result to be made again.
  • The effects tables of the SEM functions are plain data frames, as those of the other fits are. They had lavaan’s class lavaan.data.frame, whose print method rounds to three decimals.
  • tidy() returns the effects table. New tidy() methods give the table of contrasts of a result as it is stored, so identical(tidy(fit), fit$effects) is TRUE. They cover fit_solomon_glm() (four-group designs and designs with several treatments), fit_solomon_ml(), fit_solomon_mi(), fit_solomon_mmrm(), fit_solomon_sem(), fit_solomon_sem_latent(), marginal_solomon(), solomon_from_summary() (both designs), and fit_solomon_classic().
    • For compare_solomon_methods() and tipping_point_solomon(), whose table of contrasts is named results, tidy() returns results.
    • For fit_solomon_sem_latent(), tidy() returns effects, the contrasts of the four-group model; the latent ANCOVA of the pretested groups stays in effects_pre.
    • solomonR re-exports tidy() from the generics package, so it works without broom attached, and broom::tidy() uses the same methods.
    • Results with no table of contrasts have no method: equivalence_solomon(), perm_solomon(), baseline_solomon(), fit_solomon_1949(), and fit_solomon_steyn().
  • The output contract. The new help page ?solomon_output says which parts of a result are stable through v1.x, and which are not.
    • Stable: the effects table, with its columns in the order above and its contrast labels; conf_level; and tidy().
    • Not stable: fitted model objects (such as model, and the lavaan objects fit and fit_pre), settings, and the legacy elements of fit_solomon_classic().
    • It also lists the tables that cannot have the shared columns, such as analysis-of-variance tables and omnibus tests, and the results that are not tables: equivalence_solomon() returns the values of one contrast under the names of the columns, and the effects element of fit_solomon_steyn() is the last step of Steyn’s (2009) sequence, a list, not an effects table.
    The page is linked from the help page of each analysis, from the Lifecycle section of ?solomonR, and from the Package section of the reference index.
  • compare_solomon_methods() and tipping_point_solomon() return conf_level at the top level, as every other result with a table of contrasts does. For tipping_point_solomon() it is 1 - alpha, the level of the intervals in results.
  • compare_solomon_methods()$results is a table with no rows when every requested method was skipped; it was NULL. tidy() therefore returns a table for every comparison.
  • The table of report_solomon() for a fit_solomon_classic() fit has the shared columns. It is the rows of the fit’s effects table for the tests on the path; it had the columns test, estimate, and p.value alone. Code that reads its columns by name is not affected. ?solomon_output lists the table that the report of each result holds.
  • Every help page’s Value section names the elements of the result, with the columns of each table. ?fit_solomon_classic has a section on the analysis of variance. “The Classic Solomon Four-Group Analysis” shows effects and anova, and the GLM vignette points to tidy() and ?solomon_output.
  • The SEM article, the methods guide, the GLM vignette, the coverage article, and the references describe the pretest effects of the SEM fits; the simulation script of the invariance study reads the new names.
  • In benchmarks.csv of “Validation Evidence”, the estimand of the latent contrast in the invariance study is Pretest x Treatment (latent); it was Sens (latent Pretest x Treatment). Code that selects those rows by the former name needs the new one.
  • The README lists the first contrast under its label, ATE (avg over pretest), and the articles on missing data and on teaching select the rows of an effects table by label, not by position.

Reports of latent models with a newer lavaan (bug fix)

  • report_solomon() failed for latent-variable fits and invariance tests estimated by maximum likelihood without a scaled test statistic (estimator = "ML" or "MLF") once lavaan 0.7-3 was installed. That version adds Browne’s residual test to such fits, and the report took any second test to be a scaled test statistic. It now looks for a scaling factor. Reports under the default estimator (MLR) and reports made with earlier versions of lavaan were correct and are unchanged.

Credit for the unified model (#105)

  • The model of fit_solomon_glm() is now credited to Newman, Benz, and Williams (1990), who proposed it for the Solomon design: one regression for the four groups, with the pretest as a covariate coded 0 for the unpretested. The methods guide lists it as a published Solomon proposal, no longer a solomonR extension, and names the package’s additions: the four contrasts as named estimates with confidence intervals, HC3 and CR2 standard errors with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom for CR2, other families and exposure offsets, the noncollapsibility warning and marginal_solomon(), additional covariates, designs with several treatments, and randomization and equivalence tests.
  • ?fit_solomon_glm and the methods guide give the model’s source, the interaction restriction as Newman et al. printed it, and their caution against treating the unpretested as having a pretest score of zero. With the pretest now centered (#104), the pretested coefficient compares the groups at the pretested participants’ mean pretest, where Newman et al. took their adjusted means (p. 101); the four Solomon contrasts do not depend on the centering.
  • A new known-result test reproduces their worked example: the pretest slope, the within-groups sum of squares, and the tests of the treatment and the interaction (Table 3, p. 100). The printed interaction F of .22 is 0.21 from their data.
  • report_solomon() and analysis_plan_solomon() cite Newman et al.
    1. with Lin (2013) where they describe the pretest adjustment. “How to Cite solomonR” explains that fit_solomon_glm() cites them when a pretest is supplied.
  • Williams and Newman (1982), who fitted one model to all six sets of observations in answer to Campbell and Stanley, are added with Newman et al. (1990) to the history, coverage, and citation articles and the references.

Dukes et al. (1995), the latent-variable precedent (#106)

  • Dukes, Ullman, and Stein (1995), a Solomon evaluation analyzed with latent variables, is cited as a published precedent for the SEM functions in the SEM article, the methods guide, the coverage article, and the references. The SEM article sets their three two-group models, which test loadings, impose equal intercepts, and do not test the interaction, beside the package’s four-group model and invariance tests, and names what the two share. Of four further elements of their method, the pretest main effect was added under #110 (see above); the other three (a latent maturation contrast, a latent baseline check, and a standardized latent contrast) are planned under #117.

The worked example of Walton Braver and Braver (1988) (#109)

  • New data set waltonbraver1988: the hypothetical data of the worked example of Walton Braver and Braver (1988, Table 3, p. 153). Its known-result test reproduces the published Tests A, D, E, H, and I, the pretest main effect, the 1988 path, and the power remark within rounding.
  • A known-result test reproduces Tests E and H of the counterexample of Sawilowsky and Markman (1988), read in its ERIC version, and shows that its printed error entry, 1200.04, is a misprint.
  • “The Classic Solomon Four-Group Analysis” gains a section on these published worked examples, and states more precisely the reading of Test I that reproduces the published simulation rates.
  • The roadmap no longer calls the historical workflow validated. It states that the computations reproduce and the published Monte Carlo rates only in part.

Satterthwaite inference by default in fit_solomon_ml() (#115)

  • A change in default that can alter results. fit_solomon_ml() now uses inference = "satterthwaite" unless told otherwise. The point estimates are unchanged, but standard errors are larger, intervals wider, and p-values larger than under the former default, inference = "wald", most of all with small groups; a contrast that was significant before may no longer be. To reproduce results from solomonR 0.8.0 and earlier, supply inference = "wald". The change follows the package’s simulation study (#10, #22): Wald intervals had mean coverage of 0.893 with 6 participants per cell and 0.920 with 10, and the Pretest x Treatment test rejected a true null hypothesis in 7.7% of samples with 10 per cell, while Satterthwaite inference had mean coverage of 0.949 to 0.950 and Type I error of 0.050 to 0.053 at every cell size studied.
